video_title: NATO'S Accelerating Rearmament (2026) - Defence Spending, Russia & European Readiness
gist: Using newly released NATO data for 2026, the host argues alliance defence spending has jumped from just under $1.2 trillion in 2022 to just over $1.8 trillion in 2026, with almost all of the increase coming from non-US members whose equipment procurement share has surged to 33% of budgets. The core investable thesis: European NATO is now buying at a run-rate Russia cannot match in peacetime, and the surge is being deliberately channelled into building European/regional alternatives to US platforms (Patriot, Tomahawk/Typhon, E-7 Wedgetail, APKWS) rather than simply buying more American.

insights.claim: NATO alliance-wide defence spending is projected at just over $1.8 trillion in 2026 versus just under $1.2 trillion in 2022 — a roughly 50% nominal increase in four years, with the single largest annual step being the 2025-to-2026 jump of nearly $200 billion.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A ~$200bn single-year increment is the demand shock defence primes have been guiding toward; it sets the ceiling on realistic 2026-27 order intake for European and US defence contractors.

insights.claim: The one-year increase in NATO defence spending between 2025 and 2026 is roughly equal to Russia's entire annual defence budget, which the host places at $170-220 billion per year.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Frames the scale mismatch: the marginal year of Western rearmament now equals the whole of the adversary's budget, which is the core input to any long-horizon European defence thesis.
insights.quote: that would suggest that in very rough terms, the NATO alliance increased defense spending between 2025 and 2026 by about the entire Russian defense budget

insights.claim: The rearmament money is overwhelmingly non-American: from 2021 to 2026 US spending rose roughly 20% (just over $800 billion to just over $1 trillion) while the rest of NATO more than doubled, collapsing a gap that in 2021-23 saw the US outspend the whole rest of the alliance by more than 2:1 down to roughly a quarter.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The incremental defence dollar is now European, not American — a structural argument for European defence exposure over US primes on relative growth.

insights.claim: Europe's financing stack for rearmament was assembled before the Hague summit targets: the EU's SAFE programme created a €150 billion pool of low-interest, long-maturity loans, part of a wider set of measures intended to unlock roughly €800 billion, while Germany loosened its constitutional debt brake specifically to allow additional defence borrowing.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Cheap, long-dated sovereign-backed financing means the spending is less rate-sensitive than normal fiscal expansion — a reason the trend can survive a European fiscal squeeze.

insights.claim: The new NATO framework replaced the 2% guideline with a 3.5% core-defence target by 2035 plus a 1.5 percentage point 'soft defence' allowance, but the host argues the soft-defence component is largely noise because it captures spending countries would have done anyway.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Track the 3.5% core figure and discount headline 5% claims — the gap between the two is where budgetary creativity lives.

insights.claim: Stripping out inflation and FX in constant 2021 dollars, NATO spending went from $1.18 trillion in 2021, actually fell to $1.15 trillion in 2022 because of a US defence funding cut, and reaches $1.48 trillion in 2026 — a real increase of about $300 billion, of which roughly $275 billion came from non-US allies.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Roughly 92% of NATO's real spending growth is non-American, which is the cleanest single statistic supporting a European-defence overweight.

insights.claim: In real terms the alliance grew defence spending about 26% between 2021 and 2026 while the non-US allies grew closer to 77%, and over the most recent twelve months the alliance grew about 5.5% versus roughly 11% for non-US members.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A ~11% real annual growth rate for European defence budgets is the top-down sanity check against any European defence company's guided growth rate.

insights.claim: Much of the apparent US defence spending increase through 2025 was merely reversing the real-terms cuts of 2022 and 2023: in constant 2021 dollars US spending goes from about $824 billion in 2021 to only about $850 billion in 2026.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: US defence budget growth is nearly flat in real terms — a caution against extrapolating nominal US appropriations into US prime revenue growth.

insights.claim: Applying Robertson's military purchasing-power-parity multipliers steepens the NATO curve to over $2 trillion by 2026 from about $1.25 trillion in 2021, and almost entirely closes what was a nearly 2:1 US-versus-rest-of-NATO buying power advantage in 2021, though the host warns MPPP is calculated on defence spending as a whole and should not be applied to individual categories.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: MPPP is the right lens for adversary comparisons, but an import-heavy country can have a bad equipment multiplier and a great personnel one, so category-level PPP adjustments mislead.

insights.claim: The 'Danish model' of funding weapons production inside Ukraine is an explicit purchasing-power arbitrage: Denmark's military PPP multiplier is below one while Ukraine's is north of two, so transferring funds roughly more than doubles the buying power of the same money.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Explains why wealthy small NATO states will keep routing aid through Ukrainian production rather than domestic orders — a structural headwind for Nordic domestic procurement volumes.

themes.theme: National Divergence and Who Is Actually Paying

insights.claim: By 2026 the NATO members spending more of GDP on defence than the United States are Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Greece, Denmark, Sweden and Norway, with Estonia and Lithuania already hitting the 5% target on core defence spending alone.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A clean proximity screen for where procurement contracts will actually be awarded fastest over the next 24 months.

insights.claim: The 2026 second-tier spenders cluster at 2.5-2.9% of GDP — the US at 3.17%, Turkey at 2.85%, Germany at about 2.7%, then Finland, the Netherlands and the UK — while France sits at only 2.22% and Italy and Portugal at 2.1% each, with Belgium and Spain effectively at 2% and not a euro more.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The distance from 2.1% to the 3.5% target is where the largest future budget increases must come from — France, Italy, Spain and Belgium are the biggest latent upside, and the biggest political risk.

insights.claim: US defence spending as a share of GDP is actually lower in 2025 and 2026 than it was in 2021 because the defence budget has not kept pace with US economic growth driven by things like data-centre construction.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The AI capex boom mechanically dilutes the US defence-to-GDP ratio, meaning Washington's burden-sharing pressure on Europe will persist even as nominal US budgets rise.
insights.quote: If you build a ton of new data centers but not a commensurate number of new Navy warships, you get what you see on the chart there.

insights.claim: German defence spending is expected to reach about €109 billion in 2027 and grow to €183 billion a year by 2030, an increase roughly comparable in scale to the entire rise in Russian defence spending between 2023 and 2025.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Germany is the single largest euro-denominated growth pool in European defence — the primary variable in any 2027-2030 European defence revenue model.

insights.claim: The Trump administration has reportedly requested roughly $1.56 trillion in US defence spending — a $1.15 trillion base appropriation, $350 billion in reconciliation, and a $67 billion package partly to fund the war in Iran — but the host stresses Congressional approval is far from assured and doubts have been raised over at least some of the three elements.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: If it passes, the 2027 US-versus-Europe spending gap widens dramatically again; the request-versus-appropriation gap is a concrete binary event to watch for US prime multiples.

insights.claim: Every NATO member now claims to hit at least the 2% target except Slovenia, which NATO treats as a special case because it only formed a new government in June and is expected to reprogramme expenditure to comply — meaning the 2% metric has lost its discriminating power entirely.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: With the 2% floor effectively universal, analysts should switch entirely to equipment-share and 3.5% core-defence metrics to separate real rearmament from compliance accounting.

themes.theme: Equipment Share Surge — the Hard-to-Fudge Metric

insights.claim: Non-US NATO equipment spending rose from about 19% of budgets pre-Crimea and 26% in 2022 to 33% in 2026, overshooting NATO's long-standing 20% equipment target by 13 percentage points, while the US share stayed roughly flat at 28-30%.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Non-US procurement is compounding twice — bigger budgets and a bigger slice of them — and because equipment cannot be relabelled the way infrastructure can, it is the cleanest screen for genuine rearmament versus compliance accounting.

insights.claim: Non-US NATO equipment spending added about $36 billion from 2023 to 2024, another $60 billion from 2024 to 2025 and $55 billion again from 2025 to 2026, closing what was a 3:1 US advantage in 2020 to roughly $290 billion versus $260 billion in 2026.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The addressable non-US NATO equipment market has nearly reached parity with the US one — the single most important number for European defence industrial capacity investment.
insights.quote: The non- US NATO allies are now in the ballpark of spending as much on equipment in a single year as they used to spend in half a decade.

insights.claim: Poland is the procurement-intensity outlier at more than 55% of its defence budget going to equipment, with the Baltics at 40-48%, Hungary and Romania in the high 30s, the UK at 37% and France at 34%, while Slovenia sits at just over 1%.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Procurement intensity, not budget size, identifies where near-term contract flow concentrates; Poland and the Baltics punch far above their GDP weight as customers.

insights.claim: Germany's equipment share of defence spending went from 12.21% in 2016 and 17.2% in 2022 to 21% in 2024, 25% in 2025 and above 32% projected for 2026, producing a 2026 equipment spend of roughly €47 billion equivalent — about ten times the level of just over a decade ago and more than double two years ago.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Germany's equipment spend is only about 16% of the US total but covers a far narrower capability scope with no nuclear triad or global power projection, so the effective force transformation per euro is much higher.

insights.claim: NATO added just under 120,000 active-duty personnel between 2025 and 2026, led by Poland at 25,000, the United States at 24,000 and Turkey at 19,000, with Romania at 10,000 and Canada and Italy at 6,000 each — figures that exclude reservists and the earlier accessions of Sweden and Finland.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Force enlargement drives sustained demand for consumables, small arms, vehicles and basing — a longer-duration, less lumpy revenue stream than platform buys.

themes.theme: European Substitution for US Defence Products

insights.claim: The strategic logic of European rearmament is not to replace American imports outright but to ensure there is always a credible alternative, so that systems like Patriot remain a valid choice rather than the default or only choice.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Implies structural margin compression for US primes in Europe over time even as volumes hold — competition, not exclusion, is the mechanism.

insights.claim: NATO abandoned Boeing's E-7 Wedgetail as the presumptive E-3 AWACS replacement in favour of a Swedish system after the US Air Force appeared to prevaricate on the E-7, despite the E-7 offering cross-compatibility with the US and Australia.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete, already-realised example of US programmatic uncertainty directly losing a NATO-scale contract to a European supplier — the template for future losses.

insights.claim: In guided rocket kits, a recent US foreign military sale of 10,000 APKWS kits plus training and support to Saudi Arabia was priced at an estimated $1.96 billion — nearly $200,000 per rocket — while French competitors have fielded a 68mm Rafale-integrated guided rocket with only eight months from contract award to initial capability.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Cost-per-effect and speed-to-capability are becoming the competitive axis in counter-drone munitions, and European entrants are undercutting the US incumbent on both.

insights.claim: European long-range strike is emerging as a distinct procurement pool with a NATO commitment of roughly $50 billion over the next decade led by the UK, and MBDA is already pushing a ground-launched version of the French naval cruise missile that entered service in 2017 as a challenger to buying Typhon with Tomahawk.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A $50bn decade-long pool with a named European challenger to the US default is a directly investable segment; Germany buying Typhon is the incumbent case, MBDA the disruption case.

insights.claim: The Franco-Italian SAMP/T next-generation air defence system is a major beneficiary of post-2022 spending and is expected to be tested in Ukraine against ballistic targets — development the host says likely would not have happened on this timeline without the investment uptick.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A validated European ballistic-capable SAM is the key unlock for reducing Patriot dependence; watch the Ukraine test result as the gating event.

insights.claim: Joint production agreements with Ukraine are functioning as a technology-transfer accelerator into NATO industry — the UK gained an interceptor-drone lead by setting up octopus interceptor production for Ukraine, and Germany did similarly with loitering munitions and one-way attack drones.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Ukrainian co-production is a cheap option on European drone capability; firms and states with these agreements should compress development cycles versus peers.
insights.quote: the war in Ukraine and recent political environment have also provided a bit of a catalyst for the old dog that is European military industry to learn a couple of new tricks

insights.claim: US defence firms are not currently losing sales despite European substitution efforts, with global defence orders booming and order books heavily backlogged — meaning the substitution effect will show up as lost future share rather than present revenue decline.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Near-term US prime results will look fine even as the structural European share loss builds — don't use current backlog as evidence the substitution thesis is wrong.
insights.quote: a lot of order books are more backlogged than a Victorian era sewer

insights.claim: Russia's assessed military purchasing-power-parity advantage over the United States has fallen from about 3:1 in 2017 to 2.16 by 2025 under the Robertson methodology, meaning wartime cost drivers have more than offset the economies of scale from war mobilisation.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive and directly relevant: Russia's real buying power per rouble is deteriorating even as nominal spending rises, so headline Russian budget growth overstates capability growth.

insights.claim: Russian personnel costs are now in some cases more expensive than many NATO countries', with signing bonuses, debt write-offs and death payments sometimes reaching north of $70,000 US for a year of service — an inversion of the pre-war structure of poorly paid contractors and barely paid conscripts.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Personnel cost inflation is the mechanism eroding Russia's PPP edge and the single hardest line item to sustain into peacetime.

insights.claim: Even after PPP adjustment Russia's relative position has not improved: it had a bit less than half the buying power of non-US NATO members in 2022 and on 2026 projections still has about half, and less than a quarter of the alliance as a whole.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Russia's full wartime mobilisation has bought it a flat relative position against NATO's peacetime ramp — the ratio, not the level, is the decisive metric.
insights.quote: In economic and budgetary terms, then Russia is still able to dial up, but it has to pedal harder for each increase.

insights.claim: If every NATO state actually reached the agreed 3.5% core-defence target, Russia would need to spend a share of GDP comparable to North Korea or the late Soviet Union to hold the current investment ratio.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: This is the episode's central asymmetry claim and the strategic case for a multi-decade European defence spending floor.
insights.quote: If these new NATO trends and targets hold though, the math just ain't mathing.

insights.claim: Russian force expansion is structurally less sustainable than NATO's: NATO added about 150,000 active-duty personnel since 2022 through peacetime recruitment while Russia authorised roughly 400,000 via wartime enlistment bonuses, stop-loss arrangements in place since late 2022, and recruits who are older or have chronic health problems.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Implies a Russian manpower cliff whenever the war ends and wartime incentives lapse — a key input to post-war European threat assessment and defence budget durability.

insights.claim: Russia has deferred modernisation in favour of what it can build and field now: T-14 Armata is effectively absent, active protection systems are rare on main battle tanks, troop transport has devolved from BMP to Bukhanka rather than Bumerang, and despite announcing mass production in 2023 Military Balance 2026 assesses only roughly 8 to 12 Koalitsiya self-propelled guns accumulated.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Russia is consuming its Soviet inheritance rather than replacing it, while NATO buys next-generation kit targeting late-2020s to early-2030s completion — a widening qualitative gap on a defined timeline.

insights.claim: The Russian budget is showing financing stress despite Middle East conflict supporting oil prices, having cancelled multiple bond auctions due to lack of demand at acceptable interest rates and now apparently pursuing alternative financial measures.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Failed OFZ auctions are an observable, high-frequency signal of the fiscal ceiling on Russian defence spending — worth monitoring as a leading indicator.

insights.claim: The military strength of NATO's eastern flank has grown faster than the alliance overall, with the Baltics among the biggest proportional spenders, Poland adding the most personnel, and the accession of Finland and Sweden transforming the strategic geography of the region.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Concentration of capability at the flank makes the limited-incursion scenario progressively less viable, lowering the tail risk that dominates European risk premia.

insights.claim: The permanent German 45th Panzer Brigade in Lithuania functions as a deliberate tripwire: it could not stop an all-out Russian attack but all but guarantees Russia would have to kill Germans to take Lithuania, raising the odds Berlin becomes seriously involved and making grey-zone 'little green men' operations far harder to deny.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for how forward-deployed forces convert ambiguity into automatic escalation — the mechanism by which deterrence is being rebuilt on the flank.
insights.quote: in order to successfully attack Lithuania, the Russians would have to kill Germans

insights.claim: The host's 'democratization of escalation' framework holds that as eastern flank states acquire their own medium-range air defence and long-range strike, they no longer need to ask a larger ally to escalate on their behalf — Estonia could shoot down a Russian jet itself, and Poland could strike into Russia itself.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Multiplies the number of actors who can trigger escalation, which cuts both ways — it strengthens deterrence but raises the probability of an unmanaged incident.
insights.quote: the more actors involved who have the right to flip the board, the more likely it might be the board gets flipped

insights.claim: NATO's command structure remains the weak link in the autonomy story: all three joint force commands will now be run by Europeans — one by Britain, one by Italy, and one by Germany and Poland collectively — but the Supreme Allied Commander is likely to remain American and the organisation is focused on keeping the US in rather than preparing for a scenario where it is out.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Institutional dependence on US command, intelligence and enablers persists long after the spending gap closes — the real bottleneck to European strategic autonomy is not money.

themes.theme: Four Risks That Could Break the Trend

insights.claim: Risk one is that the planned increases prove fiscally or politically unsustainable: the host judges the fiscal scope exists for most states to reach 3.5% but not without trade-offs against other spending priorities or debt reduction, amid trade wars, energy crises, structural deficits and challenging demographics.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The path to 3.5% requires repeated politically costly choices, so budget durability — not budget announcements — is the risk to underwrite in long-dated defence positions.

insights.claim: Risk two is capability misallocation: most spending so far has gone into conventional major platforms — armoured vehicles, artillery, combat aircraft and warships — while Ukraine has repeatedly shown the danger of over-investing in legacy systems without a plan for enemy drones or one's own.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Suggests the drone and counter-drone segment is structurally under-allocated relative to its battlefield importance — a potential mispricing between legacy platform primes and new-entrant drone suppliers.

insights.claim: A related failure mode is buying impressive platforms without funding the magazines: a modern fighter fleet, top-tier artillery force or dense air defence network becomes largely combat ineffective as soon as munitions stockpiles run dry.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Munitions and stockpile contracts are the follow-on tranche the market may be underestimating relative to headline platform awards.

insights.claim: Risk three is defence-sector inflation eating the entire increase — the host notes defence inflation has in some places been worse than consumer inflation, and that tripling spending on shells while the cost per shell also triples buys no additional rounds.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Real deliverable volume, not budget growth, is the metric that matters; persistent defence-sector price inflation means margin expansion at primes may come at the expense of the buildup's actual output.
insights.quote: If you triple the amount you're spending on shells, but over the same time period the cost per shell also triples, you aren't actually buying more rounds.

insights.claim: Risk four is a timing mismatch on the American role: money committed in 2025 or 2026 may not become capability for years, and European alternatives to critical US systems are being developed but are not there yet, leaving a window of dependency.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The gap between US disengagement pace and European capability delivery pace is the central risk window for European security through roughly the end of the decade.
insights.quote: So the question becomes, will the United States continue to play its critical role in Europe long enough for those European investments to bear fruit?

insights.claim: The host flags that none of the presented figures include Ukraine at all, despite Ukraine having the largest army in Europe other than Russia, strong drone warfare capability and a deep magazine of long-range strike weapons — meaning the NATO-versus-Russia balance shown is conservative.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Any scenario model that excludes Ukrainian forces materially understates the combined capability facing Russia — relevant to how quickly post-war European threat perception could reset.
